list.listitem: Child abuse and neglect are prevalent medical and social issues. B
Providers have a professional and legal obligation to follow-up on clinical suspicions of child abuse or neglect. C

Suspect abuse in children with patterned bruising, bruising on certain sites (frenulum, cheeks, angle of jaw, eyelids, ear, neck or torso), and in young children. Clinicial decision rules can identify the likelihood of abuse as the cause in the event of bruising and non-vehicular head trauma under age 3 years. B
Appropriate responses should be multidisciplinary (medical, legal, mental health, and child protection). B
Efforts to strengthen and support families, improve parenting skills, and broaden supportive networks appear to be more beneficial to children than out-of-home placement. B

If not mitigated by caregiver or pediatrician, child abuse is an adverse childhood event that can permanently change the architecture of the brain, resulting in increased morbidity and mortality through associations with leading causes of death. B

Child maltreatment: Any act or series of acts of commission or omission by a parent or other caregiver that results in harm, potential for harm, or threat of harm to a child under the age of 18 years. Types of child maltreatment typically fall within the areas of physical injury, emotional injury, neglect, and sexual abuse. More recently, imminent risk of serious physical abuse and/or sexual abuse is also considered abuse under the law.
3 million reports annually, one-third of which are substantiated.
Prevalence rate of 7.4 per 1000 children.
Two-thirds of cases are in children aged less than 12 months; four-fifths are less than 3 years old.
Approximately 2000 children die annually as a result of child maltreatment (66.9% are less than 3 years of age, 44% are less than 1 year of age).
A typical family physician or pediatrician in full-time practice is likely to encounter 1 to 4 cases per year of child abuse and/or neglect in the clinical setting.
89% of cases are perpetrated by parents.
Cycles of violence (learned behaviors by perpetrators who were victims themselves or witnessed domestic violence).
Lack of parenting skills (young parents, lower educational status).
Lack of knowledge regarding child development.
Societal and cultural acceptance of corporal punishment.
Social and economic stressors (e.g., poverty, domestic violence, mental health issues, inadequate support systems, substance abuse, chronic illness, divorce, single parents).
Unresolved traumatic events in the life of the parents/caregivers that contribute to the intergenerational transmission of abuse/neglect.
Social pathology and criminal behaviors.

Acts of commission (child abuse): Overt actions or verbal exposures that cause harm, potential harm, or threat of harm and/or severe pain or seriously impair a child's physical functioning. Although injury to the child might not be intended, acts of commission are deliberate and intentional. Acts of commission include the following: Physical abuse; sexual abuse; psychological abuse.

Acts of omission (child neglect): The failure to provide for a child's basic physical, emotional, or educational needs or other essentials of life, which endangers the life or development of a child and/or impairs the child's functioning. Acts of omission include the following: Physical neglect; emotional neglect; medical/dental neglect; educational neglect; failure to supervise or provision of inadequate supervision; exposure to harmful environments.
Previous abuse, neglect, parental conflict, parental mental health, and parental substance abuse issues.
Families affected by intimate partner violence.
Children with difficult and/or challenging behaviors (conduct disorders, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and other psychological disorders).
Children with mental and/or physical impairment (developmental delays, autism, learning disabilities, etc.).
Adopted and step-children.

A US Preventive Services Task Force review of 25 studies found insufficient evidence to assess the benefit versus harm of primary care interventions (such as parent education, home visits, and referral to community resources) intended to prevent child maltreatment. Furthermore, no accurate and reliable screening tools were identified. B
The history and physical are key components to making the diagnosis of child abuse or neglect. C
Look for inconsistencies or red flags in either the history or the physical examination as well as in the timeliness of medical intervention. B
Be sure to interview the child without the caregivers present. C
Be familiar with the co-occurrence of child abuse and intimate partner violence (50% of families). B
Please refer to for Red Flag Findings and Differential Diagnosis.
Accidental trauma.

Cultural practices (e.g., cupping, likely to leave ring-shaped marks on the skin; coining, typically leaves erythematosus or hyperpigmented tracts on the skin).

Complementary and alternative therapies (herbal treatments, cupping).
Skin inflammation

Nonjudgmental approach with open-ended questions.
Child should be interviewed alone at some point during the encounter.

Concerns during history: histories that are inadequate, have irregularities, or are unlikely with regard to the mechanism of injury or the child's development; associated histories (e.g., depression, anxiety, school problems); and parental refusal to allow child to be alone with the provider.

In a pediatric ED, a 6-question screening tool administered by electronic tablet demonstrated sensitivity and specificity of 84.6% and 53.2% respectively in the identification of child sex trafficking amongst high-risk minors.
Development of abdominal pain-related disorders of gut-brain interaction (AP-DGBI) during childhood, most commonly IBS, is associated with physical, emotional, verbal abuse during childhood.
Pay attention to the child's general appearance and the interpersonal dynamics between caregiver and child.

Concerning characteristics of injury or exam include: abnormal growth or developmental criteria, suggestive patterns or types of injuries (e.g., retinal hemorrhages after 1 month old, cigarette burns, rib fractures in children less than 3 years old), multiple injuries (esp. if at different stages of healing), injuries that don't match the history or in a child who is not independently mobile, or abnormal interactions with the caregiver (e.g., observed fear of caregiver), bruising in the shape of a hand, stick, teeth mark, ligature, grip; injuries on non-bony parts of the face or body (mouth, eyes, ears, buttocks, genital, anal), injuries on neck that look like attempted strangulation, burn or scald injuries on soft tissue area that would not be expected to come into contact with a hot object, immersion (buttocks/perineum/lower limbs; stocking distribution).

If trauma is suspected, perform or consult for an ophthalmologic exam to evaluate for retinal hemorrhages (consider in children with signs or symptoms of traumatic brain injuries or shaken baby syndrome).

Validated clinical decision rules such as TEN-4-FACESp (torso, ear, neck, frenulum, angle of jaw, cheeks, eyelids, subconjunctivae, patterned) can be used to predict abuse in young children based on brusing characteristics with a sensitivity of 95.6% and specificity of 87.1%.
Serum chemistries in the setting of abdominal trauma, fractures of unknown etiology, or dehydration.
Blood counts and coagulopathy evaluations in the setting of bleeding, bruising, or anemia (e.g., CBC, bleeding time, PTT/INR).
Urinalysis in the setting of pelvic or abdominal trauma, dehydration, or acute renal failure.
Drug testing in the setting of suspected poisoning or ingestions.
Sexually transmitted disease and pregnancy testing if history or exam is suggestive of sexual abuse.

Skeletal surveys (imaging test of choice and highly recommended if <2 years old and suspicion of child abuse) or targeted x-rays of suspected fractures. Skeletal surveys should be done on infants <6 months of age with bruising, regardless of location of bruising. Skeletal surveys should be done on infants <12 months of age with bruising near eye, ear, cheek, neck, upper arm, upper leg, hand, foot, torso, buttock, or genital area.
Add-on bone scintigraphy may improve the detection rate of skeletal injury after negative skeletal survey in children suspected of physical abuse (62% vs. 52%, p <0.01, NNT = 10).
CT or MRI for suspected abdominal trauma, head trauma, or abnormal neurologic findings.
The Bruising Clinical Decision Rule or BCDR predicts the likelihood of abuse as a cause of bruising. Key elements include the site on the body, patterned bruises, and age < 5 months.
A clinical decision rule predicts the likelihood that abuse is the cause of non-vehicular head trauma in children under age 3 years.
The discussion should be child-focused and nonaccusatory. C
Stabilization of acute medical and mental health consequences of child abuse or neglect should be offered. C
Long-term management includes assurance of safety and treatment of the victim, as well as treatment and intervention for the perpetrator(s). C
Response should be multidisciplinary (medical, legal, mental health, and child protection) to ensure an effective response. B

Honesty with parent/caregiver should be encouraged as it relates to any child abuse reports that may need to be filed (once safety of the non-abusing caregiver is considered in a situation where domestic violence may be occurring). C
Providers should express concern for the child's safety and wellbeing. C

Appropriate medications for the management of acute physical and mental health consequences of child abuse or neglect should be considered (e.g., analgesia, infection, cardiovascular stabilization, emergency contraception).
Referral to local Child Protective Services is mandatory if child abuse or neglect is suspected.
Structured observation during hospitalization includes the child's response to feedings in the setting of failure to thrive, and observation of child-parent interactions.
Multidisciplinary treatment (medical, legal, mental health, and child protection) is recommended.

Injury-specific management of acute and chronic medical consequences of child abuse or neglect should be offered: 1) Medical management of acute and long-term physical consequences of abuse and/or neglect and 2) Mental health services for victims with mental health consequences of abuse and/or neglect should be offered (e.g., community-based resources with experience dealing with victims of abuse and associated mental health complications).

Perpetrators should be evaluated by the criminal justice system and offered treatment and skill-based interventions by experienced providers (mental health and community-based) to prevent future harm.
Providers should be vigilant for chronic complications associated with exposure to abuse and/or neglect.
Adolescents with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) from sexual abuse had a better response to prolonged exposure therapy compared with supportive counseling after 12 months (72% vs. 40%; NNT 3).

Authors of a Cochrane review found that compared to children in non-kinship foster care, children in kinship foster care have fewer behavioral problems (standardized mean difference effect size: −0.5; 95% CI −0.5 to −0.2), fewer mental health disorders (OR 0.5; 95% CI 0.4-0.6), and less placement disruption (OR 0.5; 95% CI 0.4-0.7). Children in non-kinship foster care were more likely to use mental health services (OR 1.8; 95% CI 1.4-2.4). Children in non-kinship foster care were more likely to be adopted (OR 2.5; 95% CI 1.4-4.5).

Trauma-informed care (TIC) is a framework to minimize the effects of trauma by addressing distress and offering emotional support to promote recovery. Greater efforts are being made to train provides in TIC to increase access for children with history of adverse childhood experience (ACE) such as child aubse.
If unrecognized and not addressed, child abuse or neglect is likely to reoccur and may be fatal or result in debilitating sequelae. B
The sequelae of child abuse or neglect may represent the acute presentation or become evident much later in the child's life or even into adulthood.

Child abuse- and/or neglect-related morbidities are products of the intensity, frequency, and chronicity of the abuse and the interplay of risk and protective factors mediating the child's response to the exposure.

Long-term sequelae include physical and mental disorders (e.g., chronic pain, physical disability, depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress disorder, suicidal ideation and intention), substance abuse, low self-esteem, relational difficulties, and risk of abuse in future relationships (interpersonal, intimate, and domestic).

In a systematic review of 19 meta-analyses with more than 20 million participatns, childhood adversity including child abuse accounted for approximately 0.5 million deaths annually in the U.S. or 15% of the total US mortality in 2019 through associations with leading causes of death.
Adults with history of childhood maltreatment as compared to those without were 3.04 times more likley to suffer from comorbid depression and cardiometabolic disease in adulthood.

Child abuse (physical, sexual, emotional, neglect, etc) is recognized as an adverse childhood experience (ACE) which can lead to permanent changes in brain architecture caused by the effects of stress response unmitigated by caregiver. This can lead to a myriad of health problems including pulmonary disease, lung cancer, liver disease, and autoimmune disease, as well as social problems including learning difficulties, decline in executive function, etc.
Regular follow-up with medical providers and multidisciplinary team members is recommended.
Education should focus on strategies to enhance child safety and prevention of future abuse or neglect.
Education should include the natural history of child abuse and neglect.
Children exposed to previous abuse, neglect, parental conflict, parental mental health issues.

The International Consensus Group on Contact Screening in Suspected Child Physical Abuse recommends that contact children, defined as asymptomatic siblings, household members, or children in the same care environment as an abused child, undergo screening. All contact children should have a history and physical exam. For children less than 1 year of age, the panel recommends a full skeletal survey and MRI of the brain (with subsequent MRI of the spine if abnormal). For children 1 to 2 years of age, the panel recommends a full skeletal survey. If there are abnormal or equivocal findings on initial imaging, repeat limited-view skeletal survey should be obtained 11 to 14 days later.
Children with speech disorders and hyperactivity, language disorders and learning disabilities, conduct disorders, and other psychological disorders.
Children with physical or mental limitations.
Adopted and step-children.

Forceful vaginal delivery, carbon monoxide poisoning, vigorous CPR, high-altitude disease, hypertensive emergencies
